newsitem.title: GREECE: MILITANT FARMERS ASK MEETING WITH GREEK PM.
newsitem.headline: MILITANT FARMERS ASK MEETING WITH GREEK PM.

text.p: Defiant farmers, playing a cat-and-mouse game with police on Greek highways, asked for a meeting with Prime Minister Costas Simitis on Thursday and vowed not to block roads for 24 hours in a show of goodwill.

"We ask for a meeting with Mr Simitis to hold an honest dialogue with no blocks on the roads," a farmers' spokesman told reporters. "If he doesn't accept us by Thursday night there will be a total black-out on highways."

Simitis has so far turned down requests by the farmers to meet, telling them flatly that his government won't bow to threats of a new blockade and that he can't satisfy their demands for cheaper fuel and state subsidies.

Farmers in central Greece played a hide-and-seek game with police for the second day on Wednesday, driving their tractors off the roads and across fields or under bridges whenever riot squads and police helicopters confronted them.
"We can block the highways whenever we choose. We have the upper hand," farmers' representative Yannis Patakis told reporters.
Police units struggled in mud and freezing temperatures all day on Tuesday, chasing tractors through vast farmlands where a number of police cars got stuck.
The farmers have vowed to repeat the crippling 25-day blockade of national roads they staged last December. Simitis has warned them he will use force to keep the roads open this time.
He sent about 5,000 police, many in riot gear, and helicopters to track down the farmers and prevent them from occupying highways.
But the farmers drove at will on to the main north-south highway and pulled back into the fields when riot police units showed up.

Main Athens newspapers were unanimous on Wednesday that the farmers had won the "first round" with the government. Ministers appeared angry as they entered an emergency cabinet meeting, chaired by Simitis, to deal with the revolt.

"This hide-and-seek game by the farmers is ridiculous and takes us many years back," Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas told reporters. "The state can't subsidise products because it's against the law, and that is that."
He accused the Greek Communist Party (KKE) of being behind the revolt, and said its political aim was to show that the government did not care for workers' problems and was authoritarian.

The farmers gave up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were not met.

Simitis, struggling to bring Greece closer to its European Union partners with a tough 1997 budget, has turned down demands by various protesting labour unions, saying the state cannot afford an extra drachma for any specific group.
